title: Meeting Buzzy Williams and the broken tenths bass
summary: Buzzy Williams, introduced by his uncle, taught him tricks including the tenths bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Yeah, he faked too. I don't know if he was a real jazz drummer, but I know he was quite an accomplished drummer. I would say that the turning point in my jazz career came when I met Buzzy Williams. Because my Uncle, Dewey Schmid, had a real good acquaintance with him. He knew him real well and told him that he would bring me and bring him out to the house and let me meet him. And I was about 11 years old or something like that, 12 at the time. I must say that Buzzy was really a wonderful person as he is today. He was not like most musicians, like a lot of the musicians in those days didn't want to help anybody. But Buzzy really was out to help anybody that he could. He showed them the little tricks that he had with that tenth bass that he used to use, a little sort of a walking bass, but instead of using octaves he used tenths. And contrary to most musicians' belief that Buzzy wasn't a good jazz man, Buzzy was quite an accomplished jazz man. It was just that his style of playing I think conflicted with bands. I mean sometimes he would interfere maybe with the blowing instruments, and a lot of musicians said that he wasn't a good band man. But he was mostly known as an accompanist for singers, because Buzzy could play on any key. And in those days that was really an accomplishment. B natural, A natural, E natural, F sharp. Keys were no problem to Buzzy. And he could transpose at sight, and that was a great help to singers. But to get back to Buzzy helping me, he showed me quite a bit of things, quite a few tricks that I even started. Still use in my cleaning today. And I'm really very grateful for the help that he gave me.
He showed you the tenth style bass, and that was way back, huh? That was, well, that was back about 1926.
In fact, I think Buzzy was probably a pioneer. They might say that Buzzy was one of the pioneers in that tenth style of bass, because he really employed it to a great extent.
There was a broken tenth, huh?

Yeah, that's right. He used broken tenths. A roll. A roll, a sort of a roll tenth. He didn't use them in his, how would you say, solid striking them simultaneously. In unison. No, he used them in broken, in broken form. That's right. He played a real, real funny style. That's why he got the nickname of Buzzy, because he was really, Buzzy was really a fast guy in these early days. And they got the same people that heard him said that he sort of made a piano hum. That's where he got the nickname of Buzzy.
Looks like they were calling a phone one.
